title: AI Agent Production Readiness: From Prototype to Operated Service
excerpt: Assess AI agent production readiness with task-level objectives, release evidence, bounded rollouts, operational ownership, and rehearsed recovery.
content:
AI agent production readiness is the ability to deliver a defined outcome under normal traffic, explain failures, and recover when dependencies or decisions go wrong. A convincing demonstration establishes that one path can work. An operated service needs evidence about the paths that fail, the people responsible for them, and the limits within which automation remains useful.

This guide proposes a readiness process for a hypothetical employee-onboarding agent. Its examples, targets, and release criteria are illustrative engineering choices, not a deployment report or universal certification standard.

## Define the service before assessing its readiness

Write a narrow service contract: given an approved onboarding request, prepare the required account changes, obtain any additional authorization, execute permitted operations, and report a verified result. Identify what remains outside scope, such as deciding employment status or approving privileged access.

Specify who can submit work, which identity establishes authority, which systems are authoritative, and what constitutes completion. “The agent answered” cannot serve as the completion contract for an account-provisioning service. Completion might require confirmed membership in three named groups, a recorded approval reference, and a customer-visible status that matches those records.

Model terminal outcomes explicitly: completed, rejected, awaiting human action, failed safely, and outcome unknown. An unknown operation result needs reconciliation ownership; it cannot disappear into a generic error counter. Also define cancellation behavior for requests already affecting external systems.

NIST’s AI RMF Core describes risk management as iterative work across governance, mapping, measurement, and management. It explicitly cautions that its actions are not a universal checklist. The framework supports organizing responsibilities; it does not certify this proposed service or replace its concrete acceptance criteria. [NIST AI RMF Core](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/).

## Express objectives in terms of useful task outcomes

Separate infrastructure health from task quality. An API can remain available while an agent provisions the wrong access. Conversely, a correct refusal can be a successful policy outcome even though no account changes occur.

For the hypothetical onboarding service, define several indicators:

| Indicator | Proposed numerator | Proposed denominator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verified completion | Eligible requests completed with required postconditions | Eligible accepted requests reaching their outcome deadline |
| Execution timeliness | Automated execution phases completed within their deadline | Execution phases admitted to automation |
| Evidence completeness | Closed requests with inspectable approval and action records | All closed requests |
| Unauthorized effects | Confirmed unauthorized changes | All admitted requests, reported with raw incident counts |

Keep the eligibility definition versioned. If difficult requests are silently excluded after failure, the completion rate becomes a marketing number. Report escalations, cancellations, unknown outcomes, and missing labels separately rather than removing them from view.

Google’s SRE guidance treats service-level objectives as tools for prioritizing reliability work and calls for stakeholder agreement and an error-budget policy. Applying that idea to agents requires choosing indicators that reflect their actual task, not copying another service’s availability percentage. [Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/).

Use two clocks when humans participate: elapsed customer time and automated processing time. Pausing the second clock for an approval wait may help diagnose computation, but it must not hide days of customer delay in the first. Publish both definitions alongside the charts.

## Assemble a release evidence packet

A readiness review should inspect artifacts rather than a slide saying “tests passed.” For this proposed service, the packet contains:

- A version manifest for code, model configuration, prompts, tools, retrieval indexes, policies, and state schemas.
- Representative evaluation results with task definitions, denominators, category breakdowns, and inspected failures.
- Authorization and isolation tests covering prohibited operations as well as allowed ones.
- Capacity evidence, including queue behavior, dependency limits, and cost controls during overload.
- Recovery evidence for interrupted runs, uncertain side effects, stale approvals, and rollback.
- Named operating owners, escalation contacts, runbooks, and a rehearsed shutdown procedure.

Link evidence to the exact candidate revision. A model configuration changed after evaluation is a different candidate, even when the application commit is identical. Record reproducible inputs where possible, while acknowledging that external model behavior and source data can change.

Anthropic’s evaluation guidance distinguishes transcripts from final environmental outcomes and emphasizes repeated trials for variable agent behavior. That distinction matters here: a fluent account-creation message is weaker evidence than verified account state. Its account is provider engineering guidance, not proof of this onboarding design. [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents).

Use [agent regression gates](/blog/ai-agent-regression-ci) to keep release evidence connected to specific candidate changes. Add manual inspection for failure classes that automated graders cannot yet assess reliably.

## Work through a bounded onboarding pilot

Assume the hypothetical team starts with read-only planning. The agent reads a request and produces proposed changes with evidence; an operator performs the actual provisioning. Compare its plans against the existing manual process on the same request families, including contractors, missing manager approvals, conflicting group names, and already-created accounts.

Suppose the next stage allows creation of one low-privilege account type for a restricted employee cohort. The proposed rollout contract requires valid approval, current employment status, a stable action identifier, and postcondition verification. Privileged groups remain outside its capabilities regardless of what the model proposes.

Illustrative goals might require 95% of eligible admitted requests to reach a verified terminal result within one business day and 99% evidence completeness. These values are chosen only to make the example concrete. The organization must decide whether its impact, workload, and recovery capacity justify them. A target of zero unauthorized effects expresses an enforcement requirement; observing none in a pilot does not establish a zero population failure probability.

Imagine 200 requests become due during the observation window. If 186 complete correctly, eight wait beyond the deadline, four need repair, and two have unknown external outcomes, verified timely completion is 186 divided by 200, or 93%. Do not call it 99% by counting only the 188 requests with resolved outcomes. Investigate each category before widening the cohort.

## Stage traffic with explicit stop conditions

Google’s canarying guidance describes evaluating a limited deployment against a control before proceeding. For an agent, the release unit may include prompts, tools, policy data, or a model selection change as well as code. A small traffic fraction alone is not protection if the selected requests can all perform high-impact actions. [Canarying releases](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/).

In the proposed onboarding rollout, constrain both volume and authority. Start with a bounded cohort and a fixed operation set, retain an unaffected comparison group, and inspect delayed outcomes before promotion. Define who can expand exposure and which evidence they must review.

Stop conditions should include unauthorized effects, missing audit records, growing unknown-outcome queues, and exhausted capacity for human review. When an alert fires, decide whether to stop new admission, revoke mutation capability, or suspend all processing. Those actions have different effects on in-flight work.

Rollback also needs a state plan. Restoring yesterday’s prompt does not undo accounts already created or make a new checkpoint readable by an old worker. Reconcile external effects and check state compatibility before resuming. The operational details belong in [agent incident response](/blog/ai-agent-incident-response).

## Make on-call ownership executable

Assign ownership for the whole task lifecycle, including approval waits and downstream uncertainty. A workflow that moves a ticket to another queue has not completed escalation until an accountable recipient accepts it. Define how long unaccepted or unresolved work may remain before another person is notified.

Run a rehearsal using a synthetic request. Let provisioning commit, discard its response, and restart the worker. The on-call engineer should find the action identity, determine whether the account exists, prevent duplicate execution, and produce an accurate customer update. Record gaps in tools and permissions discovered during the rehearsal.

Give operators a concise case view: current state, responsible owner, relevant evidence versions, pending operations, last verified effect, and allowed recovery actions. Store detailed traces separately with appropriate access controls. A wall of model text is not an incident interface.

Make the readiness decision expire when its assumptions change. New authority, a new tenant class, a different identity system, or a materially changed model can require renewed evidence. Production readiness belongs to a scoped service configuration, not permanently to a product name.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a high evaluation score mean the agent is production-ready?

No. Evaluations measure behavior under their specified tasks and environment. Readiness also requires enforceable authority, operational capacity, observability, and demonstrated recovery. Inspect category-specific failures and uncertainty rather than relying on a single score.

### Can a small team operate an agent without a dedicated platform group?

Yes, if its scope and operating commitments fit the team’s capacity. Begin with limited authority and manageable request volume. If nobody can respond to uncertain actions or maintain the evidence pipeline, reduce the service commitment before expanding autonomy.

### When should a rollout be widened?

Widen it after the agreed observation window produces sufficient task-outcome evidence, delayed cases are resolved or accounted for, and operators can handle the next cohort. Promotion should be a recorded decision against predefined criteria, not an automatic reward for a quiet dashboard.
